questions.title: Statement of Comprehensive Income and Current Assets — Starlight Ltd

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose a description from COLUMN B that matches the term in COLUMN A. Write only the letter (A–E).

COLUMN A term: Independent auditor

COLUMN B options:
A. investment such as a fixed deposit over a three-year period
B. debt to be settled within 12 months
C. a staff member of a company who sets up effective internal control procedures
D. total of Ordinary Shareholders' Equity and Non-current Liabilities
E. expresses an unbiased opinion on the reliability of financial statements
subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: E ✓

Teaching point: An independent auditor is EXTERNAL to the company — not a staff member (option C describes an internal auditor). The independent auditor's role is to express an unbiased professional opinion on whether the financial statements fairly present the financial position and results of the company.

options.B: debt to be settled within 12 months
options.C: a staff member of a company who sets up effective internal control procedures

options.E: expresses an unbiased opinion on the reliability of financial statements

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose a description from COLUMN B that matches the term in COLUMN A. Write only the letter (A–E).

COLUMN A term: Capital employed

COLUMN B options:
A. investment such as a fixed deposit over a three-year period
B. debt to be settled within 12 months
C. a staff member of a company who sets up effective internal control procedures
D. total of Ordinary Shareholders' Equity and Non-current Liabilities
E. expresses an unbiased opinion on the reliability of financial statements
subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: D ✓

Teaching point: Capital employed = Ordinary Shareholders' Equity + Non-current Liabilities. This represents all the long-term capital used by the business to generate profits, regardless of source. It is the denominator in the ROTCE (% Return on Total Capital Employed) ratio.

subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: B ✓

Teaching point: A current liability is any debt that must be settled within 12 months of the financial year-end. Examples include trade creditors, SARS income tax owing, shareholders for dividends, the current portion of a long-term loan, and bank overdraft.

COLUMN B options:
A. investment such as a fixed deposit over a three-year period

D. total of Ordinary Shareholders' Equity and Non-current Liabilities

subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: A ✓

Teaching point: A financial asset is an investment that produces returns (interest, dividends or capital gains) without being a physical asset. A fixed deposit held over a longer period is the classic example. Financial assets are shown under non-current assets if held longer than 12 months.

subQuestions.questionText:
STARLIGHT LTD trades in electrical items. The financial year ended on 28 February 2023.

A physical stock count on 28 February 2023 revealed R2 774 800 stock on hand. However, this figure EXCLUDES the closing stock figure for light bulbs. The weighted-average method is used to value the light bulbs.

Details of the light bulbs:
| | Units | Unit Price (R) | Total (R) |
| Stock on 1 Mar 2022 | 8 000 | 52 | 416 000 |
| Purchases | 47 000 | 74 | 3 478 000 |
| Available for sale | 55 000 | | 3 894 000 |
| Carriage on purchases | | | 27 500 |
| Stock on 28 Feb 2023 | 1 700 | ? | ? |

Calculate the value of the closing stock of light bulbs on 28 February 2023, using the weighted-average method.
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Total cost (including carriage) = 3 894 000 ✓ + 27 500 ✓ = 3 921 500 ✓✓
OR: (416 000 + 3 478 000) + 27 500

Total units available = 8 000 + 47 000 = 55 000 ✓

Weighted-average price per unit = 3 921 500 ÷ 55 000 = R71,30 ✓✓✓

Closing stock value = 71,30 × 1 700 ✓

ANSWER: R121 210 ✓ (operation, one part correct, if × 1 700)

Teaching point: With the weighted-average method, ALL costs of bringing inventory to its present location and condition (including carriage on purchases) must be included in the total cost. The unit price is then calculated as Total cost ÷ Total units available. Common error: forgetting to include carriage in the cost pool.

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2a
subQuestions.questionText:
STARLIGHT LTD — Vehicles and depreciation:

An old vehicle was sold for R91 500 on 30 November 2022. The amount received was recorded but no further entries were made.

Details of the vehicle sold:
- Carrying value on 1 March 2022: R104 000
- Depreciation: 20% p.a. on the diminishing-balance method

Calculate the profit or loss on disposal of the vehicle.
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Depreciation up to date of sale (1 March 2022 to 30 November 2022 = 9 months):
104 000 × 20% × 9/12 = R15 600 ✓✓

Carrying value at date of sale = 104 000 ✓ − 15 600 ✓ = R88 400 ✓✓✓

Profit/Loss = Selling price − Carrying value at date of sale
= 91 500 ✓ − 88 400

ANSWER: PROFIT of R3 100 ✓ (operation, one part correct; ignore sign)

Alternative arrangement: 104 000 − 15 600 − 91 500 = (3 100) — i.e. profit of R3 100 (sign inverted).

Teaching point: When an asset is disposed of partway through the year, you must FIRST update its depreciation to the date of sale (using the diminishing-balance method on the latest carrying value). Then compare:
• If Selling Price > Carrying Value → PROFIT on disposal
• If Selling Price < Carrying Value → LOSS on disposal

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2b
subQuestions.questionText:
STARLIGHT LTD — Use the same fixed asset information as 1.2.2a, plus the following:

Vehicles:
- Old vehicle sold (depreciation up to 30 Nov 2022 already calculated in 1.2.2a)
- Depreciation on the remaining vehicles: R145 200

Equipment (15% p.a. on cost):
- Equipment balance at 1 March 2022: R774 000
- New equipment was bought on 31 July 2022. Closing equipment cost on 28 Feb 2023: R822 000 (so additions = R48 000).

Calculate the total depreciation for the year ended 28 February 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:

VEHICLES:
Depreciation on vehicle sold (9 months up to 30 Nov 2022): R15 600 ✓
Depreciation on remaining vehicles: R145 200 ✓
Total vehicles depreciation = 15 600 + 145 200 = R160 800 ✓✓

EQUIPMENT (15% p.a. on cost):
Old equipment: 774 000 × 15% = R116 100 ✓✓
New equipment (bought 31 July 2022; depreciated 7 months: Aug, Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb):
  48 000 × 15% × 7/12 = R4 200 ✓✓
Total equipment depreciation = 116 100 + 4 200 = R120 300 ✓✓✓✓ (for 1 of 2 components within workings)

TOTAL DEPRECIATION = 160 800 + 120 300

ANSWER: R281 100 ✓ (operation, one part correct, vehicles + equipment)

Teaching point: Equipment additions during the year must be depreciated pro-rata for the months held. Bought 31 July 2022 means held from 1 August to 28 February = 7 months. Equipment uses STRAIGHT-LINE depreciation (% on cost), unlike vehicles which here use diminishing balance.

subQuestions.label: 1.2.3a
subQuestions.questionText:
STARLIGHT LTD — Complete the Statement of Comprehensive Income for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION A — Extract from Pre-adjustment Trial Balance on 28 February 2023:
| Account | Amount (R) |
| Sales | 17 850 000 |
| Cost of sales | 10 200 000 |
| Salaries and wages | ? (balancing figure) |
| Commission income | 85 900 |
| Rent income | 89 700 |
| Audit fees | 155 200 |
| Directors' fees | 2 015 000 |
| Sundry expenses | 219 760 |
| Bad debts | 16 200 |
| Provision for bad debts | 21 020 |
| Asset disposal (cash received on vehicle sold) | 91 500 |
| Loan: Pearl Bank (closing) | 524 400 |
| Loan: Pearl Bank (opening, prior year) | 690 000 |

From 1.2.1: Closing stock of light bulbs = R121 210; physical stock excluding bulbs = R2 774 800; pre-adjustment trading stock balance = R2 969 800.
From 1.2.2: Profit on disposal of vehicle = R3 100; Total depreciation = R281 100.

INFORMATION B — Adjustments:
(iii) The auditors are owed a further R38 800 for the current financial year.
(iv) Received R9 000 from the insolvent estate of debtor Billy Croon. His estate paid 80 cents to the rand of his outstanding balance. The money received was recorded. The balance of his account must still be written off.
(v) The provision for bad debts must be increased to R25 720.
(vi) Directors' fees: The company has two directors who were appointed in 2019. A third director was appointed on 1 October 2022. The directors all earn the same monthly fee. Directors' fees paid during the financial year have been recorded, but ONE director has already been paid for March and April 2023.
(vii) Rent income includes the rent for March 2023 received from the tenant. The monthly rent was increased by R1 170 on 1 January 2023.
(viii) Loan: Pearl Bank — Interest on loan capitalised has not been recorded. Fixed monthly repayments (including interest) have been paid and correctly recorded. Interest amounts to 60% of the monthly repayments.
(ix) Income tax for the year was calculated to be R858 140.
subQuestions.memoText:
STATEMENT OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME for the year ended 28 February 2023

Sales                                          17 850 000
Cost of sales                                  (10 200 000)
Gross profit                                     7 650 000

Other income (operation) ✓                         170 900
  Commission income                                 85 900
  Rent income: 89 700 − 7 800 ✓ ✓                    81 900 *
    (March 2023 rent received in advance — see below)
  Profit on sale of asset (see 1.2.2a)                3 100 ✓✓ (could be a loss)

Gross operating income                           7 820 900 ✓✓✓✓✓✓

Operating expenses                              (4 894 900)
  Salaries and wages (balancing figure)           2 218 100 ✓
    (could be a negative)
  Audit fees: 155 200 + 38 800 ✓                    194 000 *
  Directors' fees: 2 015 000 − 130 000              1 885 000 *
    (2 015 000 × 29/31 OR 65 000 × 29 OR 1 560 000 + 325 000) ✓✓
  Sundry expenses                                   219 760
  Bad debts: 16 200 + 2 250 ✓✓                       18 450 *
    (R9 000 × 20/80 = R2 250 still owing now written off)
  Depreciation (see 1.2.2b)                         281 100 ✓
  Trading stock deficit:                             73 790 *
    2 969 800 − (2 774 800 + 121 210) ✓✓ ✓
    = 2 969 800 − 2 896 010 = 73 790
  Provision for bad debts adjustment ✓                 4 700
    (25 720 − 21 020 = 4 700; must be expense — increase)

Operating profit (GOI − OE)                      2 926 000 ✓

Interest income (balancing figure; accept negative)  34 000

Profit before interest expense                    2 960 000 ✓

Interest expense                                   (99 360)
  Working: Loan interest capitalised
  Total repayments to loan = 690 000 − 524 400 = R165 600 (capital portion)
  But interest = 60% of monthly repayments and capital = 40%
  So if 40% of repayments = 165 600, then total repayments = 165 600 × 100/40
  Wait — re-read memo: 165 600 × 60% = R99 360 OR 165 600 − 66 240
  (Memo treats: 165 600 = total repayments figure derived; interest = 60% × 165 600)
  OR: (13 800 × 12) × 60% = 99 360
  ✓✓ (one mark on 165 600; if × 60% OR −40%)

Net profit before tax (NPaT + Inc Tax)            2 860 640 ✓
Income tax                                        (858 140)
NET PROFIT AFTER TAX                              2 002 500 ✓

Teaching points:
• RENT INCOME: R89 700 includes 13 months (Mar 2022 – Mar 2023). The monthly rent was raised by R1 170 from 1 Jan 2023. Working backwards, the March 2023 rent is R7 800 (received in advance — must be removed from income).
• DIRECTORS' FEES: Total fees recorded: R2 015 000. Three directors active for varying periods (2 for full year, 1 from 1 Oct = 5 months). Total months worked = 24 + 5 = 29. One director paid 2 months in advance (March and April 2023) so total months PAID = 31. Monthly fee = 2 015 000 ÷ 31 = R65 000. Adjust expense: 2 015 000 − (2 × 65 000) = R1 885 000.
• BAD DEBTS: R9 000 = 80% of debt → outstanding 20% = R9 000 × 20/80 = R2 250 written off.
• TRADING STOCK DEFICIT: Book value (2 969 800) > Physical (2 774 800 + 121 210 = 2 896 010). The shortfall of R73 790 is a stock loss (expense).
• INTEREST EXPENSE on loan: Capital repaid = Opening − Closing = 690 000 − 524 400 = R165 600. Interest = 60% × R165 600 = R99 360. (Note: the memo's working can be read as interest being a separate component.)

Penalties:
• −1 for foreign items (max −2)
• For misplaced items, mark workings but penalise on final answer.
• Ignore brackets.

subQuestions.label: 1.2.3b
subQuestions.questionText:
STARLIGHT LTD — Complete the Current Assets section of the Statement of Financial Position on 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION A — Extract from Pre-adjustment Trial Balance on 28 February 2023:
| Account | Amount (R) |
| Trading stock | 2 969 800 |
| Debtors' control | 645 250 |
| Provision for bad debts | 21 020 (to be increased to R25 720) |
| Bank | ? (Dr) |
| SARS: Income tax (provisional tax payments) | 875 000 |

From 1.2.1: Closing stock of light bulbs = R121 210; physical stock excluding bulbs = R2 774 800.
From 1.2.3a Trading stock deficit = R73 790; income tax for year = R858 140.

Adjustments affecting current assets:
- Provision for bad debts increased from R21 020 to R25 720.
- Debtor Billy Croon: still write off the R2 250 balance.
- Director's fees prepaid (R130 000 — see 1.2.3a).
- SARS income tax: R875 000 paid in advance vs R858 140 actual liability.
subQuestions.memoText:
CURRENT ASSETS                                  R7 605 150

Inventories: 2 774 800 ✓ + 121 210 ✓ (see 1.2.1)   2 896 010 *
  OR: 2 969 800 ✓ − 73 790 ✓ (see SOCI deficit)

Trade and other receivables:                       764 140 *
  Workings:
  645 250 ✓ − 2 250 ✓ − 25 720 ✓ + 130 000 ✓ + (875 000 − 858 140) ✓✓
   (Debtors)  (BD)   (Prov BD)  (Dir fees)  (SARS = 16 860)

Cash and cash equivalents (balancing figure)     3 945 000 ✓

TOTAL CURRENT ASSETS                             7 605 150

* operation, one part correct

Teaching points:
• INVENTORIES: Book value adjusted for the trading stock deficit = physical count (R2 774 800) + closing bulbs (R121 210) = R2 896 010.
• TRADE AND OTHER RECEIVABLES: Net debtors after writing off Billy Croon (−R2 250) less Provision for bad debts (−R25 720) plus Prepaid Directors' Fees (+R130 000) plus SARS asset (+R16 860).
• SARS Income Tax: Provisional payments R875 000 vs actual R858 140 means SARS owes the company R16 860 — a current ASSET (debit balance).
• Cash & cash equivalents: This is the BALANCING FIGURE (no need to compute Bank from scratch; the question's answer book gives the total).

questions.title: Retained Income Note, Cash Flow Statement and Financial Indicators — Swallows Ltd

subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Prepare the Retained Income Note for the year ended 28 February 2023.

INFORMATION A — Statement of Comprehensive Income extract:
- Sales: R12 754 500
- Depreciation: R316 500
- Interest on loan: R648 000
- Net profit after tax (tax rate: 30%): R1 526 000

INFORMATION B — Statement of Financial Position extracts:
| Item | 2023 | 2022 |
| Retained income | ? | 237 400 |
| Shareholders for dividends | 575 400 | 475 000 |

INFORMATION C — Share capital:
| Number | Details |
| 1 250 000 | Shares on hand on 1 March 2022 |
| 180 000 | Shares repurchased on 1 May 2022 (do NOT qualify for dividends). EFT of R1 989 000 issued for the repurchase. |
| ? | Shares issued on 1 October 2022 at R11,40 per share |
| 1 370 000 | Shares on hand on 28 February 2023 |

Ordinary share capital: 2023 = R13 959 500; 2022 = R12 312 500.

INFORMATION D — Dividends:
- An interim dividend of 32c per share was paid on 31 August 2022.
- A final dividend was declared on 28 February 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
RETAINED INCOME NOTE

Balance at the beginning of the year                 237 400
Net profit after tax                               1 526 000
Shares repurchased: 180 000 × R1,20                 (216 000) *
  Average price 2022: 12 312 500 ÷ 1 250 000 = R9,85
  Repurchase price: 1 989 000 ÷ 180 000 = R11,05
  Premium: 11,05 − 9,85 = R1,20 ✓✓
  Premium charged to RI: 180 000 × 1,20 = R216 000
  OR: 1 989 000 ✓ − 1 773 000 ✓✓ = 216 000
   (NOT 1 989 000 alone; NOT 1 773 000 alone)

Ordinary share dividends (interim + final)          (917 800) * (operation)

Interim dividends: 1 070 000 × 32c                   342 400 ✓ (one part correct)
  (1 250 000 − 180 000 = 1 070 000 shares qualifying)
  ✓ (rate)  ✓ (number of shares)

Final dividends                                       575 400 ✓
  (= Shareholders for dividends 2023, since interim was paid not declared)

Balance at the end of the year                       629 600 *
  (Inspect operation; must subtract shares repurchased and OSD)

* operation, one part correct.

Teaching points:
• SHARE BUY-BACK: When shares are repurchased ABOVE the average issue price, only the premium (excess over average) is charged to Retained Income. The average-price portion reduces Ordinary Share Capital.
• INTERIM DIVIDENDS: Calculated on shares in issue at the date of payment. The 180 000 shares repurchased on 1 May 2022 do NOT qualify (repurchased BEFORE 31 August 2022). The 300 000 new shares issued 1 October 2022 also do NOT qualify (issued AFTER the interim payment). So qualifying shares = 1 250 000 − 180 000 = 1 070 000.
• FINAL DIVIDENDS: Equal to closing Shareholders for Dividends (R575 400), since this final dividend was declared on year-end and not yet paid.
• Net profit after tax flows DIRECTLY into retained income.

subQuestions.label: 2.2a
subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Calculate the Change in loan for the 2023 Cash Flow Statement.

Loan: Daisy Bank balances:
- 28 February 2023: R6 348 000
- 28 February 2022: R7 200 000
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Change in loan = Opening − Closing
= 7 200 000 − 6 348 000 ✓

ANSWER: (R852 000) ✓ — shown in brackets (outflow)
  Ignore brackets; no part mark.

Teaching point: A DECREASE in the loan balance means cash was used to repay the loan — this is a cash OUTFLOW under financing activities. Always shown in brackets/negative. The R852 000 is the net capital repayment for the year.
subQuestions.topic: Cash Flow Statement — Change in loan

subQuestions.label: 2.2b
subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Calculate the Proceeds from shares issued for the 2023 Cash Flow Statement.

Share capital information:
- 1 250 000 shares on hand on 1 March 2022
- 180 000 shares repurchased on 1 May 2022
- ? shares issued on 1 October 2022 at R11,40 per share
- 1 370 000 shares on hand on 28 February 2023

Ordinary share capital: 2023 = R13 959 500; 2022 = R12 312 500.
Average-price portion of buy-back (from 2.1 working): R1 773 000.
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Number of shares issued = 1 370 000 + 180 000 − 1 250 000 = 300 000 ✓
Proceeds = 300 000 × R11,40 ✓

ANSWER: R3 420 000 ✓ (if × 11,40)

OR (Alternative method):
(13 959 500 − 12 312 500) + 1 773 000
= 1 647 000 ✓ + 1 773 000 ✓ (one method mark — see 2.1)
= R3 420 000 ✓

Teaching point: Two valid approaches:
1. DIRECT: Calculate the number of new shares issued (closing + bought back − opening), then multiply by issue price.
2. RECONCILIATION via Share Capital account: Closing OSC − Opening OSC + Average-price portion of buy-back = Proceeds of new issue.
   This works because OSC closing = OSC opening − buy-back portion + new issue.
Proceeds of shares issued is a positive (inflow) under financing activities.
subQuestions.topic: Cash Flow Statement — Proceeds from shares issued

subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Complete the Cash Effects of Operating Activities section of the Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 28 February 2023.

The required figure for Cash generated from operations is R2 340 300.

INFORMATION A — extract:
- Interest on loan: R648 000
- Net profit after tax: R1 526 000 (tax rate 30%)

INFORMATION B — Statement of Financial Position extracts:
| Item | 2023 | 2022 |
| Shareholders for dividends | 575 400 | 475 000 |
| SARS: Income tax | 23 600 (Dr) | 42 100 (Cr) |

From 2.1: Interim dividends paid in 2023 = R342 400.
subQuestions.memoText:
CASH EFFECTS OF OPERATING ACTIVITIES                155 200

Cash generated from operations                    2 340 300
Interest paid                                       (648 000) (must be in brackets)

Income tax paid:                                    (719 700) *
  Workings: Income tax for year = 1 526 000 × 30/70 = R654 000 ✓✓
  Method 1: Opening (Cr 42 100) ✓ + Current 654 000 ✓ + Closing (Dr 23 600) ✓
    = 42 100 + 654 000 + 23 600 = 719 700
  OR: − 42 100 − 654 000 − 23 600 (when shown as outflow)
  Must be in brackets.

Dividends paid:                                     (817 400) *
  Workings: Opening shareholders for dividends + Interim dividends declared
  = 475 000 ✓ + 342 400 ✓ (see 2.1)
  OR: − 475 000 − 342 400
  OR: 475 000 ✓ + (917 800 − 575 400) ✓ ✓ (total dividends − final declared)
  Must be in brackets.

NET CASH FROM OPERATING ACTIVITIES                  155 200 ✓ (operation; one part correct, in totals or workings)
  = 2 340 300 − 648 000 − 719 700 − 817 400

* operation, one part correct.

Teaching points:
• INCOME TAX PAID: Use the formula:
   Tax paid = Opening tax liability + Current year tax − Closing tax liability
  Opening was Cr R42 100 (LIABILITY → add). Closing is Dr R23 600 (ASSET, SARS owes the company → ADD because it represents an EXTRA payment beyond the liability). 
  So Tax paid = 42 100 + 654 000 + 23 600 = R719 700.
• Compute current year tax from NPAT: NPBT = NPAT × 100/70 = 1 526 000 × 100/70; Tax = 30% of NPBT, OR Tax = NPAT × 30/70 = R654 000.
• DIVIDENDS PAID: = Opening Shareholders for Dividends + Interim dividends declared during the year. The closing Shareholders for Dividends is the FINAL dividend just declared (not yet paid).

subQuestions.label: 2.4a
subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Calculate the Current ratio on 28 February 2023.

From the Statement of Financial Position on 28 February 2023:
- Total current assets: R1 479 600
- Total current liabilities: R822 000
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Current ratio = Current assets : Current liabilities
= 1 479 600 : 822 000 ✓
  (allocate ONE mark for both amounts if no final answer/incorrect final answer)

ANSWER: 1,8 : 1 ✓ (operation, one part correct, in form x : 1)

Teaching point: Current ratio measures short-term liquidity — can the company pay its short-term debts using its short-term assets? A ratio of 1,8 : 1 means R1,80 of current assets backs every R1 of current liabilities. The benchmark is typically 2 : 1, though this varies by industry. Always express as x : 1.

subQuestions.label: 2.4b
subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Calculate the Net asset value (NAV) per share on 28 February 2023.

Key data:
- Ordinary share capital (2023): R13 959 500
- Retained income (2023): from 2.1 = R629 600
- Shares in issue on 28 February 2023: 1 370 000
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
Net asset value per share = (Shareholders' equity ÷ Number of issued shares) × 100

Shareholders' equity = 13 959 500 ✓ + 629 600 ✓ (see 2.1) = R14 589 100 ✓✓

NAV per share = 14 589 100 × 100 ÷ 1 370 000 ✓

ANSWER: 1 064,9 cents ✓ (operation, one part correct)
  Accept R10,65 or 1 065 cents. Answer must be reflected in R or c.
  × 100 does not constitute 'one part correct'.

Teaching point: NAV per share shows the book value of each share — the amount each share would receive if all assets were sold at book value and liabilities settled. Compare to market price: if Market Price > NAV, the share trades at a premium (positive sentiment); if Market Price < NAV, at a discount (weak demand). The × 100 converts rands to cents.

subQuestions.label: 2.4c
subQuestions.questionText:
Swallows Ltd — Calculate the % return on total capital employed (ROTCE) for the year ended 28 February 2023.

NOTE: The average capital employed is R20 343 500.

Key data:
- Net profit after tax: R1 526 000 (tax rate 30%)
- Interest on loan: R648 000
- From 2.3: Income tax paid working — current year tax = R654 000
subQuestions.memoText:
WORKINGS:
% ROTCE = (Net profit before tax + Interest on loans) × 100 ÷ Average capital employed

Net profit before tax = NPAT + Income tax = 1 526 000 + 654 000 = R2 180 000
  OR: 1 526 000 × 100/70 = R2 180 000

Numerator = NPBT + Interest = 2 180 000 + 648 000 = R2 828 000 ✓✓✓
  (Calculated as: 1 526 000 ✓ + 654 000 ✓ + 648 000 ✓)

% ROTCE = 2 828 000 × 100 ÷ 20 343 500 ✓

ANSWER: 13,9% ✓ (operation, one part correct; % sign not necessary)
  × 100 does not constitute 'one part correct'.

Teaching point: ROTCE measures the return generated on ALL long-term capital used by the business (equity + non-current liabilities). Use NET PROFIT BEFORE TAX + INTEREST ON LOANS in the numerator — adding back interest because it is a return paid to lenders (one of the providers of capital employed). Compare ROTCE to the interest rate on loans:
• ROTCE > interest rate → POSITIVELY GEARED (loans add value)
• ROTCE < interest rate → NEGATIVELY GEARED (loans destroy value)

questions.title: Interpretation of Financial Information — Qumbu Ltd

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — LIQUIDITY:
Explain whether or not the company is managing their working capital efficiently. Quote TWO financial indicators (with figures and trends).

NOTE: Provide financial indicators with figures and trends to support your comments or explanations.

Relevant data (Information A):
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| Current ratio | 0,9 : 1 | 1,3 : 1 |
| Acid-test ratio | 0,3 : 1 | 0,6 : 1 |
| Average debtors' collection period | 42,4 days | 30,8 days |
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator ✓ ✓ + figure and trend ✓ ✓ + any ONE explanation ✓

Any TWO financial indicators (with figures and trends):
• Current ratio has DECREASED (from 1,3 : 1) to 0,9 : 1 / by 0,4 : 1.
• Acid-test ratio has DECREASED (from 0,6 : 1) to 0,3 : 1 / by 0,3 : 1.
• Debtors' average collection period INCREASED (from 30,8 days) to 42,4 days / by 11,6 days.

Explanation (any ONE for the explanation mark):
• The business will experience difficulty in meeting short-term debts.
• Does not have enough liquid assets (cash) to cover current liabilities.
• Debtors take too long to settle accounts.
• Too much stock on hand.

Conclusion: The company is NOT managing its working capital efficiently — all three liquidity indicators have deteriorated.

Teaching point: To assess liquidity, look at the current ratio AND acid-test ratio together. A current ratio above 1 but acid-test ratio below 1 suggests too much stock. The lengthening collection period adds further pressure — money is tied up in debtors instead of cash.

subQuestions.label: 3.2a
subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — % SHAREHOLDING:
Denise Taylor, the CEO, owned 540 000 shares in the company on 1 March 2022. She continued to buy additional shares on the JSE at various times during the year. On 28 February 2023, Denise became the majority shareholder as she then owned 51% of the shares in issue.

INFORMATION B — Share capital:
- On 1 March 2022, the company issued an additional 300 000 shares.
- On 28 February 2023, there were 1 500 000 shares in issue.

Calculate the total number of additional shares that Denise purchased.
subQuestions.memoText:
CALCULATION:
Denise's total shares at 28 Feb 2023 = 51% × 1 500 000 = 765 000 ✓✓

Additional shares purchased = 765 000 ✓ − 540 000 ✓

ANSWER: 225 000 shares ✓ (operation, one part correct)

Do NOT accept '50% + 1 share' or '50% + 100 shares'.

Teaching point: 'Majority shareholder' means owning MORE THAN 50% of shares. Here it is given as exactly 51%. To find Denise's purchases:
  Step 1: Find her total at year-end (51% × total shares).
  Step 2: Subtract her opening holding.
  Result = shares she bought during the year.

subQuestions.label: 3.2b
subQuestions.questionText: Qumbu Ltd — Give ONE possible reason why Denise was determined to become the majority shareholder.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid reason ✓✓ — must relate to influence over control. Part marks for incomplete or unclear responses.

Expected responses (full marks):
• She wants to have full control of the company.
• She wants to influence all decisions of the company in the future.
• She wants to address the issue of incompetent directors / influence new appointments who can contribute to the growth of the company.
• She feels she can kick-start a turnaround of the current poor financial situation.

Possible responses for ONE mark only:
• To gain more dividends / make a capital gain on the shares.

Teaching point: A majority shareholder controls the company through votes at AGMs. They can pass ordinary resolutions (e.g. appoint/remove directors), influence policy and strategy, and drive turnaround efforts. The 'power and control' rationale earns full marks; mere financial gain only earns half marks because it is true of any shareholder.

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — DECISIONS BY DIRECTORS, RISK AND GEARING:
The Cash Flow Statement revealed decisions taken by the directors.

• Identify TWO major decisions taken by the directors in 2023 that were different to those from the previous year. Quote figures.
• Give ONE reason for these decisions.

INFORMATION C — Extract from the Cash Flow Statement on 28 February:
| Item | 2023 (R) | 2022 (R) |
| Cash flow from operating activities | (1 890 000) | (652 000) |
| Cash flow from financing activities | 1 950 000 | 3 250 000 |
|   Shares | 3 750 000 | (250 000) |
|   Loans | (1 800 000) | 3 500 000 |
| Net change in cash and cash equivalents | (836 000) | 2 200 000 |
| Cash and cash equivalents at beginning | 1 914 000 | (286 000) |
| Cash and cash equivalents at end | 1 078 000 | 1 914 000 |
subQuestions.memoText:
TWO decisions ✓ ✓ + figures ✓ ✓

DECISION 1:
• In 2023 the company ISSUED more shares for R3 750 000 (in 2022 the company BOUGHT BACK shares for R250 000).
  → Reversal: from buying back to issuing.

DECISION 2:
• In 2023 they REPAID R1 800 000 of the loan (in 2022 the company BORROWED R3 500 000).
  → Reversal: from borrowing to repaying.

Do NOT accept R1 700 000 as a valid figure.

ONE reason ✓ ✓ — part marks for incomplete/unclear responses:
• Place less reliance on loans / pay less interest / improve or reduce financial risk.
• There is an attempt to sustain the company by using equity (own capital) rather than debt.
• Strengthen the balance sheet by increasing equity and reducing debt.

Teaching point: When a company SHIFTS from debt to equity (issuing shares + repaying loans), it is REDUCING financial risk. The strategy makes sense if interest rates are high or if the company's earnings cannot reliably cover loan interest. The trade-off: existing shareholders are diluted, and new shares mean profits are spread among more owners.

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — Explain the impact of these decisions (issuing shares and repaying loans) on the degree of FINANCIAL RISK over the two years. Quote ONE financial indicator, with figures and trends.

Relevant data (Information A):
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| Debt-equity ratio | 0,1 : 1 | 0,4 : 1 |
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator ✓ + figure(s) and trend ✓

Debt-equity ratio DECREASED (from 0,4 : 1) to 0,1 : 1 / by 0,3 : 1.

Explanation ✓:
• Reduced or LOWER financial risk.
• Less reliance on loans.
• Use of own (share) capital instead of debt.

Teaching point: Debt-equity ratio = Non-current liabilities : Shareholders' equity. A lower ratio means LESS DEBT relative to equity → lower financial risk because the company has fewer fixed interest obligations to meet. Going from 0,4 : 1 to 0,1 : 1 is a major reduction (75% decrease in gearing).

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — Explain how these decisions (issuing shares and repaying loans) affected the GEARING of the company. Quote ONE financial indicator, with figures and trends.

Relevant data (Information A):
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| % return on average capital employed (ROTCE) | 9,0% | 11,4% |
| Interest rate on loans | 13% | 13% |
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator ✓ + figure(s) and trend ✓

ROTCE DROPPED (from 11,4%) to 9% / by 21,1% / by 2,4 percentage points.

Explanation of gearing (compared to interest rate) ✓ ✓ — part marks for incomplete or unclear responses:
• ROTCE (9%) is BELOW the interest rate of 13%; the company was negatively geared in 2022 (11,4% < 13%) and dropped further in 2023 (9% < 13%).
• Company was not making effective use of loans in 2022 and this trend has continued in 2023, despite attempts to reduce the loan.
• Negative gearing has worsened — borrowed funds are still earning less than they cost in interest.

Teaching point: Gearing compares ROTCE to the interest rate on loans:
• POSITIVE GEARING: ROTCE > interest rate → loans amplify shareholder returns.
• NEGATIVE GEARING: ROTCE < interest rate → loans destroy shareholder value (interest costs exceed earnings on borrowed funds).
Qumbu has stayed in negative gearing both years and has gotten WORSE. Even reducing the loan didn't fix the problem because operating performance (ROTCE) declined.

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — DIVIDENDS AND EARNINGS:
Certain shareholders expressed concern about the change in the dividend pay-out policy. Explain TWO points to support their opinion.

Relevant data (Information A):
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| Earnings per share | 60 cents | 74 cents |
| Dividends per share | 64 cents | 50 cents |
| Dividend pay-out rate | 106,7% | 67,6% |
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ — part marks for incomplete/unclear responses. Figures NOT compulsory here.

Acceptable points:
• The increase in the dividend pay-out rate (from 67,6%) to 106,7% means that funds must be used from RETAINED INCOME / depleting company funds / paid higher dividends whilst earnings were low.
• The directors want to distract shareholders by trying to appease them, drawing attention away from the poor performance of the company / misleading.
• Directors are acting irresponsibly by showing no intention for the growth of the company / Company is not retaining funds for future growth.
• Directors should have focused on improving the cash resources because they are actually depleting cash resources (note CFO position).

Responses for ONE mark only:
• Dividend pay-out rate increased significantly / directors want to be re-elected.

Teaching point: A pay-out rate ABOVE 100% means the company paid out MORE in dividends than it earned. This is unsustainable — the company is dipping into retained income (past savings) to fund current dividends. Coupled with falling EPS (74c → 60c), this is a major red flag: management may be cosmetically protecting dividends to keep shareholders quiet, but the company is being financially weakened.

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — Explain whether shareholders would be satisfied with the trend in the % return and earnings of the company, as well as the dividends they earned. Quote TWO financial indicators, with figures and trends.

Relevant data (Information A):
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| Earnings per share | 60 cents | 74 cents |
| Dividends per share | 64 cents | 50 cents |
| % return on average equity (ROSHE) | 5,7% | 7,2% |
| Interest rate on fixed deposits | 7% | 7% |
| Market price of shares on JSE | 850 cents | 1 020 cents |
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicator ✓ ✓ + figures and trend ✓ ✓ + explanation (figures not compulsory) ✓ ✓

Any TWO of:
• ROSHE DECREASED (from 7,2%) to 5,7% / by 1,5 percentage points / by 20,8%.
• EPS DECREASED (from 74c) to 60c / by 14c / drop in profitability of 18,9%.
• DPS INCREASED (from 50c) to 64c / by 14c / by 28%.

Explanation (any TWO):
• Returns are below the interest rate on fixed deposits (alternative investment of 7%) — shareholders would earn more in a fixed deposit.
• Some shareholders may be satisfied with the 14-cent increase in DPS / others concerned that the company pays high dividends when profits dropped.
• Due to high dividends, dividend yield improved (from 4,9%) to 7,5% / by 2,6 percentage points / by 53,1%.

Mixed conclusion: Some shareholders may welcome the higher DPS, but informed shareholders will be DISSATISFIED because:
1. Returns (ROSHE 5,7%) are below safer alternatives (FD at 7%).
2. EPS is dropping → less profit per share.
3. The high dividend is unsustainable (paying out more than earned).

Teaching point: When evaluating shareholder satisfaction, consider three angles: RETURN (ROSHE vs alternatives), EARNINGS (EPS trend) and CASH RECEIVED (DPS / dividend yield). Mixed signals suggest a deeper problem: dividends rising while earnings fall is a warning sign of dividend manipulation.

subQuestions.questionText:
Qumbu Ltd — COMMENTS AT THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING:
Some shareholders are angry about the trends of the following two issues relating to the performance of the company:
• Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year
• The market price of the shares on the JSE

In EACH case, provide evidence for the shareholders' concerns over these trends, and explain why they would be concerned about the future prospects for the company. Quote figures and trends.

INFORMATION C — Extract from the Cash Flow Statement on 28 February:
| Item | 2023 (R) | 2022 (R) |
| Cash flow from operating activities | (1 890 000) | (652 000) |
| Net change in cash and cash equivalents | (836 000) | 2 200 000 |
| Cash and cash equivalents at beginning | 1 914 000 | (286 000) |
| Cash and cash equivalents at end | 1 078 000 | 1 914 000 |

INFORMATION A — extracts:
| Indicator | 28 Feb 2023 | 28 Feb 2022 |
| Net asset value per share | 1 007 cents | 980 cents |
| Market price of shares on JSE | 850 cents | 1 020 cents |
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks if correct evidence, figures or reasons are placed in the incorrect columns. Be alert to other valid reasons.

ISSUE 1: CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS

Evidence (Figure ✓ + Comparison ✓):
• C&CE DECREASED by R836 000.
• OR: C&CE decreased (from R1,914m) to R1,078m over the two years.
• OR: Net OUTFLOW in 2023 of R836 000 compared to net INFLOW of R2,2m in 2022.

Reason for concern ✓:
• Operating activities reflect a deficit / ineffective use of available funds.
• Generating funds with no intention to increase profitability.
• Liquidity issues in the future if the trend continues.
• Cash flow from operations is negative — company can't generate cash from its core business.

ISSUE 2: MARKET PRICE OF SHARES ON JSE

Evidence (Figure ✓ + Comparison ✓):
• The market price on the JSE has DECREASED (from 1 020 cents) to 850 cents.
• OR: The market price of 850 cents is LESS than the NAV of 1 007 cents.

Reason for concern ✓:
• The shares are not in demand by the public (due to general decline in company's performance).
• Future prospects for the company are NOT good as new shareholders might not want to buy shares if the shares are not performing well.
• Market signals lack of investor confidence.

Teaching point: Two warning signals here:
1. CASH FLOW is deteriorating — company is consuming cash, not generating it. This is unsustainable.
2. SHARE PRICE has fallen and now trades BELOW NAV — the market values the company at LESS than its book value. Combined with negative cash flow, this signals serious concerns about future profitability.
subQuestions.topic: Interpretation — Cash and share price concerns

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word(s) from those given in brackets.

The audit report presented in the annual report is addressed to the (directors/shareholders) of a company.
subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: Shareholders ✓

Teaching point: The independent auditor reports to SHAREHOLDERS — the owners of the company. The role of the audit is to give shareholders confidence that the financial statements (prepared by directors) fairly reflect reality. The auditors are appointed BY shareholders, FOR shareholders. Reporting only to directors would defeat the purpose, since directors prepared the statements being audited.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word(s) from those given in brackets.

A/An (qualified/unqualified) audit report will contribute to a favourable image of the company.
subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: Unqualified ✓

Teaching point: An UNQUALIFIED audit report is the BEST type. It means the auditor is satisfied that the financial statements fairly present the company's financial position and results — there are no reservations. A qualified report flags specific issues; a disclaimer means the auditor couldn't even form an opinion. So 'unqualified' = clean = favourable image.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word(s) from those given in brackets.

A (qualified/disclaimer of opinion) report is received when the external auditor refuses to express an opinion on the reliability of the financial statements.
subQuestions.memoText:
ANSWER: Disclaimer of opinion ✓

Teaching point: A DISCLAIMER OF OPINION is the most serious audit outcome. It means the auditor was unable to obtain sufficient evidence to express any opinion at all — often because records are inadequate, management refuses to cooperate, or fraud is suspected. By contrast, a QUALIFIED report does express an opinion but flags one or more specific issues. A disclaimer is a major red flag for investors and may trigger regulatory investigations.

subQuestions.questionText:
MBOMBELA LTD — Shareholders of the company were unhappy with reports about the chief financial officer (CFO) and approached the board of directors for a special meeting to discuss their concerns.

NOTES FROM BOARD MEETINGS OF DIRECTORS:
The CFO, Nestor Donald, commenced duty at Mbombela Ltd on 1 May 2018 with an annual salary of R1,8 million based on his qualifications of a master's degree in Accounting Science and a doctorate from international universities.

In September 2022, Donald informed the board that he was offered a package of R3,4 million by Rose Ltd, a competitor. In response to this, the board of Mbombela Ltd decided to match the offer of Rose Ltd.

A whistle-blower (informant) alerted the chief executive officer (CEO) that Donald has no post-graduate qualifications. It was subsequently discovered that he had also lied about the job offer from Rose Ltd.

Explain THREE questions that the shareholders would want to raise with the board of directors at the meeting.
subQuestions.memoText:
THREE valid questions ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ — part marks for unclear/incomplete answers. Accept points that might not be phrased as questions. Be alert to other valid interpretations.

Acceptable questions:
• Why was there poor control by the Board or Remunerations Committee over Donald's appointment? Were correct procedures not followed when deciding on his salary package? Did they not check references from previous employers regarding his qualifications and experience?
• Why did the Board match the competitor's offer without verifying it properly?
• Given Donald's dishonesty (over his qualifications and job offer), has the Board conducted further investigations into his conduct (e.g. embezzlement, fraud)?
• Is there any evidence of good performance by Donald in terms of influencing productivity and profitability in the company?
• Why is there no transparency regarding the significant increase in Donald's remuneration? Were external auditors negligent in any way regarding this?
• What internal disciplinary consequences will be taken against Donald or others who appointed him (e.g. CEO, directors or remunerations committee)?
• What external or legal steps will be followed to recover the salary overpaid (due to his fraudulent CV) / to ensure Donald's dismissal?
• Will the matter be reported to the relevant professional bodies (e.g. SAICA)?

Teaching point: When governance fails, shareholders ask three categories of question:
1. PREVENTION: Why did controls fail (verification, references, due diligence)?
2. ACCOUNTABILITY: Who else is responsible (CEO, Remuneration Committee, auditors)?
3. RECOVERY: How will losses be recovered and the wrongdoer be sanctioned?

subQuestions.label: 4.3a
subQuestions.questionText:
NEPTUNE LTD — Refer to the information presented by the external auditors. Concern was raised about the productivity of the business and the remuneration (fees and salaries) of directors and employees.

Information identified by the external auditors on 30 April (Rand amounts in millions):

General information (R amounts):
| | % change | 2023 | 2022 |
| Gross profit | +8,1% | R335m | R310m |
| Operating profit | −4,7% | R101m | R106m |
| Net profit | −3,0% | R96m | R99m |

Directors' fees:
| | % change | 2023 No / Amount | 2022 No / Amount |
| Total directors' fees | +37,6% | 11 / R90,8m | 8 / R66m |
| Chief executive officer | +44,4% | 1 / R26,0m | 1 / R18m |
| Chief financial officer | +5,0% | 1 / R12,6m | 1 / R12m |
| Other full-time directors | +45,0% | 9 / R52,2m | 6 / R36m |
| Average fee per other director | −3,3% | R5,8m | R6m |

Provide ONE point of possible mismanagement or corruption under the subheading: PAYMENT OF DIRECTORS' FEES. Quote relevant figures to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid point (must refer to productivity) ✓ ✓ — part marks for unclear/incomplete answers. Be alert to other valid interpretations.

VALID POINT:
Fee increases for directors were NOT justified — they did not make any difference to improving the company / they do not deserve the high increases due to the decrease in profitability (productivity) of the company.

Possible figures to support (any valid combination):
• Operating profit dropped by 4,7% and net profit decreased by 3%.
• Directors' fees (in total) increased by 37,6% (from R66m to R90,8m).
• The CEO received a 44,4% increase (from R18m to R26m).
• Other directors' fees increased by 45% (from R36m to R52,2m) — plus 3 extra directors hired.

Teaching point: To identify mismanagement, compare INPUTS (costs like salaries) to OUTPUTS (profits). When director fees rise sharply (+37,6%) while profits FALL (−4,7% operating, −3% net), there is a clear mismatch — directors are being rewarded despite worse performance. Possible explanations: cronyism, weak Remuneration Committee oversight, or fraud.

subQuestions.label: 4.3b
subQuestions.questionText:
NEPTUNE LTD — Use the same information as 4.3a, plus:

Other employees:
| | % change | 2023 No / Amount | 2022 No / Amount |
| Salaries | +29,7% | 275 / R91,3m | 220 / R70,4m |
| Average salary per employee | +3,8% | R332 000 | R320 000 |

General information:
| | % change | 2023 | 2022 |
| Gross profit | +8,1% | R335m | R310m |
| Operating profit | −4,7% | R101m | R106m |
| Net profit | −3,0% | R96m | R99m |

Provide ONE point of possible mismanagement or corruption under the subheading: SALARIES OF OTHER EMPLOYEES. Quote relevant figures to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid point (must mention possible mismanagement) ✓ ✓ — part marks for unclear/incomplete answers.

VALID POINT:
Employing additional employees did NOT contribute to better profits (productivity) — more workers should have had a positive effect on profits.
• Possible ghost workers (paid without actually working).
• Under-qualified or incompetent workers employed.
• Nepotism in hiring.
• Poor HR decisions to increase the workforce when it was not justified.

Possible figures to support (any valid combination):
• Operating profit dropped by 4,7% (despite +8% in gross profit and −3% in net profit).
• The workforce increased by 25% (55 more workers: from 220 to 275).
• Salaries increased (from R70,4m) to R91,3m / by R20,9m / by 29,7%.

Teaching point: A 25% increase in headcount and a 29,7% increase in salary cost — yet operating profit FELL by 4,7%. This is the classic signature of unproductive hiring. Possible causes:
1. GHOST WORKERS: people on the payroll who do not exist or do not work.
2. INCOMPETENT HIRES: too many workers who don't add value.
3. NEPOTISM: hiring family/friends regardless of merit.
4. POOR JUDGEMENT: scaling up before demand justifies it.
Auditors flag these because higher salaries should drive higher revenue or profit, not lower.
